strengths: The paper makes a meaningful contribution to interpretability security: feature visualizations can be redirected through weight fine-tuning within standard architectures. The initialization-to-target tunnel and gradient-matching objective provide a clear methodological advance over conspicuous architectural fooling circuits.

The core vulnerability is convincingly demonstrated across CNNs, vision transformers, datasets, and visualization procedures. In Table 1, ResNet-50 target-image CLIP similarity increases from 0.53 to 0.69 while accuracy decreases from 76.13% to 75.13% and feature AUROC remains 1.00 at the reported precision. Attacks on ten additional output neurons and transfer to MACO strengthen the evidence.

The accuracy–manipulation sweeps, model-size experiments, target-image analysis, and direct ProxPulse comparison provide useful evidence about the attack's behavior. The weapon-classifier example illustrates a consequential application while preserving the deliberately poisoned classification behavior.

The presentation is generally clear, and the appendices document model sources, preprocessing, optimization settings, visualization procedures, and computational resources. An implementation is linked, although its contents were not independently verified here. Limitations and potential misuse are explicitly discussed, with no evident material ethical concerns. The demonstrated vulnerability and practical method support acceptance.
weaknesses: Preservation of internal representations and mechanisms is claimed more strongly than demonstrated. Classification accuracy and feature AUROC establish limited behavioral properties; AUROC primarily measures class ranking. The non-target FV comparisons in Appendix D.3 also provide only indirect evidence. In the CLIP experiment, w=1 in Table 11 removes the full-representation preservation term from Eq. (11). Held-out activation comparisons and causal feature interventions would substantiate the stronger preservation claims.

The claim of producing arbitrary target images needs qualification. Higher-resolution results frequently reproduce textures or composition rather than the specified image, out-of-distribution targets perform less well, and some narrow models suffer very large accuracy losses. The experiments establish compelling examples of semantic redirection, but do not establish reliable arbitrary-image reconstruction across feature–target pairs.

The theory primarily explains an idealized construction. Lemma 3.1 assumes an exactly prescribed quadratic field and unregularized gradient ascent; it provides no approximation-error guarantee for the trained networks or activation-matching variant. Eq. (5) can also be discontinuous at the tunnel boundary, and the universal-approximation citation does not establish accurate gradient approximation within a fixed architecture. These distinctions should be clearer when describing the theoretical support.

The auditing and defense conclusions exceed their evaluation. The case study attacks a manually constructed concept direction without executing the proposed feature-discovery and attribution audit. Natural-image activation maximization is a sensible cross-check, but top-ranked examples and before/after Jaccard overlap do not establish a deployable detector: there is no decision threshold, clean-model false-positive evaluation, or adaptive-attack assessment. Claims that discovery becomes effectively impossible or that defense effectiveness is quantitatively established should be narrowed.

Comparative and statistical coverage could be stronger. ProxPulse is evaluated on one feature–target pair with two reported trade-off settings, which limits conclusions about broad superiority. The reported standard deviations describe repeated FV generation from manipulated models, rather than variability across independent attack-training runs. A matched tuning budget and repeated fine-tuning runs would better establish reliability.

Several reporting details require reconciliation. Table 3 specifies 100 FV runs, whereas Appendix C.8 specifies 30 for CLIP; Section 5 reports a 0.1% ImageNet preservation subset, whereas Table 10 reports 0.28%. The sampling geometry also needs clarification: the stated radius of 0.01 would not encompass typical high-dimensional Gaussian initializations with per-coordinate standard deviation 0.01 under the usual Euclidean norm.
